rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the transgressing human as Abu Jahl; some say the whole surah concerns him, others only from the prohibition scene onward.
rows.anchor: أكثر المفسرين على أن المراد من الإنسان ههنا إنسان واحد وهو أبو جهل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: While the Prophet prayed, Abu Jahl threatened him; his boast about having the largest gathering occasioned the summons of his assembly and the zabaniya, who would seize him if he summoned them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يصلي فجاء أبو جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reminding a human made from a clot of his origin should prevent arrogance; Abu Jahl instead grew more defiant through wealth and Meccan leadership.
rows.anchor: لما عرفه أنه مخلوق من علق فلا يليق به التكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jahl reportedly said no one in Mecca was more honored than he; the commentator conjectures this answered the description of God as most generous.
rows.anchor: ويروى أنه قال : ليس بمكة أكرم مني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some deny that the whole surah was among the earliest revelations; others say the first five verses came first and the rest later about Abu Jahl, then God ordered them joined.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون خمس آيات من أول السورة نزلت أولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an example of later material being joined to earlier revelation, commentators call 2:281 the last-revealed verse although it was attached to older material.
rows.anchor: { واتقوا يوما ترجعون فيه إلى الله }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although reports make Abu Jahl the more apparent referent, the surface context more closely supports humanity generally: despite creation and blessings, people transgress through sin and appetite, and face judgment.
rows.anchor: القول الأول وإن كان أظهر بحسب الروايات ، إلا أن هذا القول أقرب بحسب الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla is a rebuke restraining the human who repays God's favor with transgression, though the object of rebuke is implicit in context.
rows.anchor: أنه ردع وزجر لمن كفر بنعمة الله بطغيانه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Kalla means the human fails to recognize that God created him from a clot and taught him after ignorance, because wealth absorbs him in worldly love.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : كلا لا يعلم الإنسان إن الله هو الذي خلقه من العلقة

rows.speaker: الجرجاني صاحب النظم
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani reads kalla as an affirmative ‘indeed,’ since nothing before or after it supplies an object for a rebuttal; he compares its use in 74:32.
rows.anchor: ذكر الجرجاني صاحب النظم أن { كلا } ههنا بمعنى حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Transgression means arrogance and rebellion; love of wealth, status, abundance, and power is the root cause of heedlessness toward the surah's proofs of divine unity, power, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: الطغيان هو التكبر والتمرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic lām in the prediction about Abu Jahl exceeds the wording about Pharaoh because the latter command preceded Moses' encounter, evidence, and Pharaoh's divinity claim, whereas this passage consoles Muhammad after rejection.
rows.anchor: وههنا ذكر في أبي جهل : { ليطغى } فأكده بهذه اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's unbelief remained verbal despite his power, while Abu Jahl, despite lesser standing, sought to kill and harm the Prophet; this makes the stronger emphasis fitting.
rows.anchor: فرعون مع كمال سلطته ما كان يزيد كفره على القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh first treated Moses well and eventually professed faith, unlike Abu Jahl, who envied Muhammad from youth and died hating him.
rows.anchor: وأما أبو جهل فكان يحسد النبي في صباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beloved Prophet is to the interlocutor Moses as the eye to the hand; people guard the eye more, so the warning is more emphatic here.
rows.anchor: الحبيب في مقابلة الكليم كاليد في مقابلة العين

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash parses the clause as ‘because he saw him,’ with the lām of li-anna deleted.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش : لأن رآه فخذف اللام

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains the omission of ‘himself’: raʾā governs a noun and predicate like verbs of supposition, and Arabic omits nafs with this verb class.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء إنما قال : { أن رءاه } ولم يقل : رأى نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading of istaghna is that the human considers wealth sufficient without his Lord, but this cannot explain everyone: Solomon and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf remained humble when wealthy.
rows.anchor: استغنى بماله عن ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentator rejects treating wealth itself as necessarily producing arrogance: a rational person sees greater dependence on God when rich, since he must preserve himself, wealth, and dependents.
rows.anchor: العاقل يعلم أنه عند الغنى يكون أكثر حاجة إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn in istaghna can mark seeking: a person imagines his effort earned wealth rather than God's gift and enabling; many who strive die hungry, and the wealthy will learn their riches were not their own achievement.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية وجه ثالث : وهو أن سين { استغنى } سين الطالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens by praising knowledge and ends by condemning wealth, thereby urging religion and learning and turning people away from worldly wealth.
rows.anchor: أول السورة يدل على مدح العلم وآخرها على مذمة المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address turns toward the human as a threat and warning about the consequence of transgression.
rows.anchor: واقع على طريقة الالتفات إلى الإنسان تهديدا له وتحذيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-rajʿā means return or reference and is among the verbal nouns of returning.
rows.anchor: { الرجعى } المرجع والرجوع وهي بأجمعها مصادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the human will see the reward of obedience and punishment for rebellion; the warning cites God's delay of wrongdoers until the day eyes stare, and benefits sincere believers more than heedless people.
rows.anchor: أنه يرى ثواب طاعته وعقاب تمرده وتكبره وطغيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively God returns people from maturity and wealth to weakness, poverty, and death, just as He raised them from inanimate state and poverty to life, wealth, and honor.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى يرده ويرجعه إلى النقصان والفقر والموت

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abu Jahl sarcastically proposed making Mecca's mountains gold and silver so people could take riches, become transgressors, abandon their faith, and follow Muhammad; Gabriel offered this, warning that rejection would bring the punishment of the Table's companions, so the Prophet refrained to spare them.
rows.anchor: روى أن أبا جهل قال للرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام : أتزعم أن من استغنى طغى

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abu Jahl asked whether Muhammad prayed among them and swore to trample his neck; seeing Muhammad pray, he recoiled, then said a fiery trench and terror lay between them.
rows.anchor: روى عن أبي جهل لعنه الله أنه قال : هل يعفر محمد وجهه بين أظهركم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports that Umayya ibn Khalaf used to forbid Salman from praying.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أن أمية بن خلف كان ينهى سلمان عن الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent referent is the human already mentioned, explaining the Abu Jahl reports; revelation could concern him while applying generally, though what follows implies a particular man.
rows.anchor: ولا يمتنع أن يكون نزولها في أبي جهل ، ثم يعم في الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Araʾayta addresses the Prophet in astonishment: after he prayed for Islam to be strengthened through Abu Jahl or Umar, God points out the absurdity of expecting help from someone who forbids prayer.
rows.anchor: اللهم أعز الإسلام إما بأبي جعل بن هشام أو بعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title Abu al-Hakam is ironic: someone who prevents worship of the Lord and prostrates to idols is not fit to be called wise.
rows.anchor: كان يلقب بأبي الحكم ، فكأنه تعالى يقول : كيف يليق به هذا اللقب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is the height of folly for a man who is neither creator nor lord to command others and forbid them from obeying their actual Lord and Creator.
rows.anchor: يعتقد أنه يجب على الغير طاعته ، مع أنه ليس بخالق ولا رب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ‘a servant’ signifies Muhammad's perfected devotion; preventing the most devoted servant from worship is utter ignorance. A report has Ali describe his character through the contrast between worldly goods and the Prophet's divinely praised character.
rows.anchor: أن التنكير في عبدا يدل على كونه كاملا في العبودية

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Asked by an eloquent Jewish visitor to describe Muhammad's manners, Ali asks him to describe worldly goods first; when he cannot, Ali contrasts their fewness with God's praise of the Prophet's great character.
rows.anchor: فلما سأل عليا عنه قال : صف لي متاع الدنيا حتى أصف لك أخلاقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite expression also condemns Abu Jahl's habitual practice of forbidding anyone he saw from praying.
rows.anchor: أن هذا أبلغ في الذم لأن المعنى أن هذا دأبه وعادته

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: When Ali saw people praying before the Eid prayer, he would not forbid them, fearing that he might fall under this threat.
rows.anchor: روى عن علي عليه السلام أنه رأى في المصلى أقواما يصلون قبل صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa followed this courteous indirectness: when Abu Yusuf asked whether a worshipper should say ‘forgive me’ on rising from bowing, he gave the prescribed praise and prostration without explicitly forbidding it.
rows.anchor: وأخذ أبو حنيفة منه هذا الأدب الجميل حيث قال له أبو يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jahl should not imagine God would lack another worshipper if Muhammad did not prostrate: countless proximate angels continually pray and glorify God.
rows.anchor: ولي من الملائكة المقربين مالا يحصيهم إلا أنا وهم دائما في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite servant also magnifies Muhammad, who is understood despite lacking an earlier explicit mention, as with the unintroduced servant in the Night Journey and other verses.
rows.anchor: أنه تفخيم لشأن النبي عليه السلام يقول : إنه مع التنكير معرف

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first view makes both araʾayta passages address the Prophet; their matching addressee preserves the discourse's rhetorical order, and asks whether the unbeliever might instead follow guidance and care for himself.
rows.anchor: أنه خطاب للنبي عليه السلام ، والدليل عليه أن الأول وهو قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that reading, a rational, prosperous man would do better to choose faith, guidance, and enjoining piety than disbelief and forbidding worship; the passage laments his lost higher station.
rows.anchor: أما كان ذلك خيرا له من الكفر بالله والنهي عن خدمته وطاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second view addresses the unbeliever: God, like a judge or master hearing opposing parties, turns from the Prophet to ask whether he would forbid a man whose prayer guides and commands piety.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أنه خطاب للكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer and calling others to God are the two things that troubled Abu Jahl, so both are named.
rows.anchor: الذي شق على أبي جهل من أفعال الرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام هو هذان الأمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was always either reforming himself through prayer or reforming others by commanding piety.
rows.anchor: إما في إصلاح نفسه ، وذلك بفعل الصلاة أو في إصلاح غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's prayer itself was guidance and an exhortation to piety: witnessing it softened hearts and inclined people to faith, making action a stronger call than speech.
rows.anchor: فكان فعل الصلاة دعوة بلسان الفعل ، وهو أقوى من الدعوة بلسان القول

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading addresses the Prophet: the preceding proofs are clear and reason shows it is wrong to stop a servant serving his Lord; one who denies them and obstructs worship acts in stubbornness, despite knowing God sees.
rows.anchor: أنه خطاب مع الرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام ، وذلك لأن الدلائل التي ذكرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative addresses the unbeliever: if Muhammad is lying or turning away, would he not know that God sees him and stop, rather than need your prohibition?
rows.anchor: والثاني : أنه خطاب للكافر ، والمعنى إن كان يا كافر محمد كاذبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse threatens resurrection and complete requital: God knows everything, is wise, and nothing as small as an atom escapes Him, so He will fully repay each person, frightening sinners and encouraging the obedient.
rows.anchor: المقصود من الآية التهديد بالحشر والنشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed about Abu Jahl, everyone who prevents obedience to God shares his warning.
rows.anchor: وإن نزلت في حق أبي جهل فكل من نهى من طاعة الله فهو شريك أبي جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat does not condemn forbidding prayer in a usurped house or disliked times: what is forbidden is the accompanying transgression, not prayer itself.
rows.anchor: لأن المنهى عنه غير الصلاة وهو المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A master may prevent a slave's night prayer or voluntary fast, and a husband his wife's retreat, to secure her interest with her Lord's permission, not out of hostility to worship.
rows.anchor: لأن ذلك لاستيفاء مصلحته بإذن ربه لا بغضا لعبادة ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla can rebuke Abu Jahl for forbidding God's worship and commanding worship of al-Lat.
rows.anchor: أنه ردع لأبي جهل ومنه له عن نهيه عن عبادة الله تعالى وأمره بعبادة اللات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Abu Jahl will fail to kill Muhammad or trample his neck; Muhammad's follower will kill him and trample his chest.
rows.anchor: كلا لن يصل أبو جهل إلى ما يقول إنه يقتل محمدا أو يطأ عنقه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says kalla means he does not know God sees; even if he knows, failure to act on that knowledge makes him as one who does not know.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : كلا لا يعلم أن الله يرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lanasfaʿan may mean seize the forelock and drag him to Hell; the same verb is used of seizure by forelocks and feet.
rows.anchor: لنأخذن بناصيته ولنسحبنه بها إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other lexical interpretations are striking his face, blackening it (the Khalil's gloss for a light scorching), or humiliating him; blackening signifies disgrace.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل : تقول للشيء إذا لفحته النار لفحا يسيرا يغير لون البشرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies Abu Jahl with the man branded on the snout, giving another reading of the forelock's punishment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في قوله : { سنسمه على الخرطوم } إنه أبو جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic doubled-nūn reading makes God and the angels the agents, as in the verse naming God, Gabriel, and the righteous as allies.
rows.anchor: قرىء لنسفعن بالنون المشددة ، أي الفاعل لهذا الفعل هو الله والملائكة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's reading, la-asfaʿanna, has God say to Muhammad that He Himself will take charge of Abu Jahl's humiliation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود لأسعفن ، أي يقول الله تعالى يا محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened seizure may happen in the afterlife or worldly life; one report says Abu Jahl lunged at the Prophet during prayer but recoiled from a fiery trench or an open-mouthed beast, with Gabriel and Michael also described as lions on the Prophet's shoulders.
rows.anchor: ما روى أن أبا جهل لما قال : إن رأيته يصلي لأطأن عنقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report has Ibn Masud recite al-Rahman to Quraysh, be struck and have his ear split by Abu Jahl, then find him dying at Badr and stab his snout from afar, perhaps fulfilling the mark on the snout.
rows.anchor: فافتتح قراءة السورة ، فقام أبو جهل فلطمه فشق أذنه وأدماه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: At Badr Abu Jahl taunts Ibn Masud as a little shepherd; Ibn Masud replies that Islam rises and is never overcome, and Abu Jahl says Muhammad remained his greatest enemy in life and death.
rows.anchor: يا رويعي الغنم لقد ارتقيت مرتقى صعبا

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: On hearing Abu Jahl's final hatred, the Prophet reportedly called him more Pharaoh-like than Moses' Pharaoh, who had at least professed belief.
rows.anchor: فرعوني أشد من فرعون موسى فإنه قال { ءامنت } وهو قد زاد عتوا

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abu Jahl asked Ibn Masud to behead him with his own sharper sword; Ibn Masud could not carry the head because of his weakness, so dragged it by a thread through the split ear.
rows.anchor: ثم قال لابن مسعود : اقطع رأسي بسيفي هذا لأنه أحد وأقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentator offers three explanations for Abu Jahl's weakness: as a dog he should be dragged, his split ear warranted ear-for-ear retaliation, and dragging his head forward fulfilled the forelock threat; he says he gives the report's meaning, not exact wording.
rows.anchor: هذا ما روى في مقتل أبي جهل نقلته معنى لا لفظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forelock is forehead hair, or the place where it grows; here it stands metonymically for face and head. Abu Jahl cared for grooming and perfuming it, so God threatens to blacken it and his face.
rows.anchor: كنى ههنا عن الوجه والرأس بالناصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite forelock is physically known but its attributes are newly exposed: it is false in speech and sinful in action.
rows.anchor: الناصية المعروفة عندكم ذاتها لكنها مجهولة عندكم صفاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forelock is called lying because Abu Jahl lied about God not sending Muhammad and called the Messenger a sorcerer, liar, or non-prophet; another explanation is his boast of having the largest assembly.
rows.anchor: وإنما وصف بالكذب لأنه كان كاذبا على الله تعالى في أنه لم يرسل محمدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is called sinful because its owner rebels against God; khāṭiʾ is culpable, unlike mukhṭiʾ, who is not held to account, and the adjective follows the usage of describing faces as gazing.
rows.anchor: والفرق بين الخاطىء والمخطىء أن الخاطىء معاقب مؤاخذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second naṣiya is an appositive for the definite first one; an indefinite can replace a definite when it is qualified and supplies an independent point.
rows.anchor: { ناصية } بدل من الناصية ، وجاز إبدالها من المعرفة وهي نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading with nominative naṣiya implies ‘it is a forelock’; the accusative and nominative can both serve as invective.
rows.anchor: قرىء ناصية بالرفع والتقدير هي ناصية ، وناصية بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Prophet rebuked Abu Jahl and recited these verses, Abu Jahl boasted of his large assembly of dependents; this prompts the challenge to summon it and God's counter-summons.
rows.anchor: قال : يا محمد بمن تهددني وأني لأكثر هذا الوادي ناديا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Nadi means the people of a gathering, not the place itself, which is only called a gathering when its people are present; it derives from people resorting and assembling, as at Mecca's Dar al-Nadwa.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : ناديه أي أهل مجلسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation calls it the gathering of generosity; the phrase sarcastically invites Abu Jahl to summon his supposed noble, generous defenders.
rows.anchor: وقيل : سمي ناديا لأنه مجلس الندى والجود

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والمبرد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Mubarrad give zabaniya's singular as zabniya, from pushing; the word can describe a rebellious human or jinn, like ifriya.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة والمبرد : واحد الزبانية زبنية وأصله من زبنية إذا دفعته

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash transmits zabani as one proposed singular; others propose zabin.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش : قال بعضهم واحده الزباني ، وقال آخرون : الزابن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical view treats zabaniya as a plural with no singular in the same form, like ababil and abadid.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : هذا من الجمع الذي لا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended beings are powerful angels of punishment; Muqatil describes them as Hell's keepers, with feet on earth and heads in heaven.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة فالمراد ملائكة العذاب

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the zabaniya are Hell's keepers, whose legs are on earth and heads in heaven.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : هم خزنة جهنم أرجلهم في الأرض ورؤسهم في السماء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says zabaniya means police in Arabic and describes the harsh, strong angels who push unbelievers into Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : الزبانية هم الشرط في كلام العرب وهم الملائكة الغلاظ الشداد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are called zabaniya because they push unbelievers into Hell.
rows.anchor: ملائكة النار سموا الزبانية لأنهم يزبنون الكفار أي يدفعونهم في جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading dares Abu Jahl to call his supporters against Muhammad, while God summons zabaniya beyond his people's power; Ibn Abbas says they would seize him immediately, and other readings place his dragging in this world at Badr or in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: الأول : أي فليفعل ما ذكره من أنه يدعو أنصاره ويستعين بهم في مباطلة محمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that if Abu Jahl summoned his assembly, the zabaniya would seize him at once, visibly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : لو دعا ناديه لأخذته الزبانية من ساعته معاينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reverses the order: God will seize the forelock and summon the zabaniya in the afterlife, so Abu Jahl may then call his assembly to try to stop them.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني : أن في الآية تقديما وتأخيرا أي لنسفعا بالناصية وسندع الزبانية في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ in ‘let him summon his assembly’ signals a miracle: the challenge invites the unbeliever to call them, which would trigger God's counter-summons; his failure to dare shows the Prophet's miracle.
rows.anchor: الفاء في قوله : { فليدع ناديه } تدل على المعجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A passive reading, sutdaʿā, means ‘will be summoned’; this is certain divine action, especially as a promise to avenge the Prophet, and the future tense recalls the promise to help even after a time.
rows.anchor: قرىء : { * ستدعى } على المجهول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading is not an expression of uncertainty: God's promise is bound to occur, as the prophetic assurance says, ‘I will help you even after a while.’
rows.anchor: فائدة السين هو المراد من قوله عليه السلام : ( لأنصرنك ولو بعد حين )

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla rebukes Abu Jahl: his boastful assembly cannot help him, he is too weak to resist the Prophet, and he will not make the Prophet obey his ban on prayer; it may also mean ‘no, do not obey him.’
rows.anchor: وهو ردع لأبي جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not obey Abu Jahl, as in the parallel prohibition against obeying deniers.
rows.anchor: وهو كقوله : { فلا تطع المكذبين }

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Most exegetes interpret ‘prostrate’ as pray and devote oneself to God's worship through action and preaching, without fretting over the enemy because God will support the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وعند أكثر أهل التأويل أراد به صل وتوفر على عبادة الله تعالى فعلا وإبلاغا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some interpret ‘prostrate’ more generally as submission or humility.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : بل المراد الخضوع

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others understand the command as the physical prostration in prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : بل المراد نفس السجود في الصلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Approaching means seeking nearness to God through prostration; a prophetic report says a servant is closest to his Lord while prostrating.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث : ( أقرب ما يكون العبد من ربه إذا سجد )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation addresses Abu Jahl: Muhammad should prostrate and Abu Jahl approach to see the zabaniya seize him, with the prayer increasing the unbeliever's rage as believers' devotion enrages them.
rows.anchor: اسجد يا محمد ، واقترب يا أبا جهل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On a further sarcastic reading, Abu Jahl is told to put his foot on the praying Prophet, who is occupied with himself; the taunt belittles Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: ثم قال عند ذلك : { واقترب } منه يا أبا جهل وضع قدمك عليه

none: surah heading and verse quotation only

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that the unexpressed object of ‘We sent it down’ is the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: أجمع المفسرون على أن المراد : إنا أنزلنا القرآن في ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaving Qur'an implicit magnifies it in three ways: God claims the act as His own, an emphatic pronoun replaces an unnecessary famous name, and the time of revelation is exalted.
rows.anchor: لأن هذا التركيب يدل على عظم القرآن من ثلاثة أوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural is majesty, not multiple gods: divine unity is proved, and multiple fully powerful gods would each be dispensable, while less-than-fully powerful ones would be deficient.
rows.anchor: فعلمنا أن قوله : { أنا } محمول على التعظيم لا على الجمع

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says the Qur'an's descent began on Laylat al-Qadr because the prophetic mission began in Ramadan.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي : ابتداء بإنزاله ليلة القدر لأن البعث كان في رمضان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the whole Qur'an descended to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr and then came to earth in installments; the commentator answers that its descent to heaven counts as arrival, and could kindle anticipation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : أنزل إلى سماء الدنيا جملة ليلة القدر ، ثم إلى الأرض نجوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the anticipation explanation, heaven is shared between angels and humans: their dwelling, our roof and adornment, so sending the Qur'an there is like sending it here.
rows.anchor: السماء كالمشترك بيننا وبين الملائكة ، فهي لهم مسكن ولنا سقف وزينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line illustrates that longing is strongest when destinations draw near; the poet is not named.
rows.anchor: وأبرح ما يكون الشوق يوما إذا دنت الديار من الديار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadr is the verbal noun of determining and refers to what God ordains; qadr and qadar share the root, with one vocalization a verbal noun and the other a noun. Al-Wahidi glosses it as proportioning without excess or deficiency.
rows.anchor: القدر مصدر قدرت أقدر قدرا ، والمراد به ما يمضيه الله من الأمور

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: One explanation names it the night of determining affairs: God assigns the coming year's rain, provision, life, and death, then reveals these already-eternal decrees to angels and records them on the Preserved Tablet; most scholars choose this view.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء ، عن ابن عباس : أن الله قدر ما يكون في كل تلك السنة من مطر ورزق وإحياء وإماتة

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri interprets qadr as greatness and honor, supported by the following verse; the honor may accrue to worshippers or to the acts of worship themselves.
rows.anchor: الثاني : نقل عن الزهري أنه قال : { ليلة القدر } ليلة العظمة والشرف

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq says the night is named for the honored Book sent through an honored angel to an honored community; the commentator suggests the surah repeats qadr three times for this reason.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بكر الوراق سميت : { ليلة القدر } لأنه نزل فيها كتاب ذو قدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another answer takes ‘in Laylat al-Qadr’ to mean that the remembrance was sent down in the night's honor and excellence.
rows.anchor: والوجه الثالث في الجواب : أن التقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third proposed meaning is a constricted night, because the earth is crowded by angels.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث : ليلة القدر ، أي الضيق فإن الأرض تضيق عن الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealment resembles God's hiding His pleasure among acts, answered prayer, greatest name, middle prayer, accepted repentance, and death, to make people pursue all good and fear; similarly, it encourages reverence for every Ramadan night.
rows.anchor: فكذا أخفى هذه الليلة ليعظموا جميع ليالي رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people knew the night, temptation might lead them to sin knowingly, whose penalty outweighs the reward of obedience; concealing it prevents harm, just as the Prophet's mercy toward a sleeping man spared him a worse offense.
rows.anchor: فكانت معصيتك مع علمك أشد من معصيتك لا مع علمك

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: When the Prophet saw a sleeping man in the mosque, he asked Ali to wake him for ablution; Ali asked why the Prophet had not done it himself, and the Prophet said refusal to Ali would not be disbelief, which would lessen the man's culpability.
rows.anchor: يا علي نبهه ليتوضأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God also hides the night so seekers earn the reward of striving to find it.
rows.anchor: أن العبد إذا لم يتيقن ليلة القدر ، فإنه يجتهد في الطاعة في جميع ليالي رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uncertainty makes people worship throughout Ramadan, allowing God to boast before angels who objected that humans corrupt and shed blood; this reveals the wisdom of God's answer that He knows what they do not.
rows.anchor: فكيف لو جعلتها معلومة لها فحينئذ يظهر سر قوله : { إني أعلم * مالا * تعلمون }

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says the day shares the night of Qadr's merit, since naming two nights in a vow of retreat entails their days; day and night alternate.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي : نعم يومها كليلتها

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says that if the night is virtuous only because the Qur'an descended then, it occurred once and has ended; the majority hold that it continues.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل : من قال إن فضلها لنزول القرآن فيها يقول انقطعت وكانت مرة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reportedly said that someone who keeps worship through the whole year will find Laylat al-Qadr.
rows.anchor: روى عن ابن مسعود أنه قال : من يقم الحول يصبها

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies the night with the blessed night of innocence, using the description in 44:3.
rows.anchor: وفسرها عكرمة بليلة البراءة في قوله : { إنا أنزلناه فى ليلة مباركة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority restrict it to Ramadan: since the Qur'an is said to descend in Ramadan and on Laylat al-Qadr, the two statements must coincide.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أنها مختصة برمضان

rows.speaker: ابن رزين
rows.claim: Among date proposals, Ibn Razin names the first night of Ramadan.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن رزين : ليلة القدر هي الليلة الأولى من رمضان

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Hasan al-Basri proposes the seventeenth night because the morning after was the Battle of Badr.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن البصري : السابعة عشرة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report traced to the Prophet places it on the nineteenth night.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس مرفوعا التاسعة عشرة

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ishaq assigns it to the twenty-first night.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق : الحادية والعشرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas assigns it to the twenty-third night.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس الثالثة والعشرون

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud assigns it to the twenty-fourth night.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود : الرابعة والعشرون

rows.speaker: أبو ذر الغفاري
rows.claim: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari assigns it to the twenty-fifth night.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو ذر الغفاري : الخامسة والعشرون

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب وجماعة من الصحابة
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group of Companions assign it to the twenty-seventh night; some propose the twenty-ninth.
rows.anchor: وقال أبي بن كعب وجماعة من الصحابة : السابعة والعشرون

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: The argument for the first night includes Wahb's report that Abraham's scriptures descended on the first of Ramadan, then the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel on the twelfth and eighteenth of Ramadan, with long intervals between revelations.
rows.anchor: قالوا : روى وهب أن صحف إبراهيم أنزلت في الليلة الأولى من رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That argument continues that the Qur'an descended annually on each Qadr night to the lowest heaven before its twenty-year revelation to the Prophet; because Ramadan held these blessings, its first night was called Qadr.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله تعالى القرآن في عشرين شهرا في عشرين سنة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i leaned toward the twenty-seventh night based on a report about water and mud.
rows.anchor: مال الشافعي إليه لحديث الماء والطين

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question ‘What made you know?’ means the hearer's knowledge cannot reach the full excellence and ultimate greatness of Laylat al-Qadr; the surah then gives three proofs of its merit.
rows.anchor: يعني ولم تبلغ درايتك غاية فضلهاومنتهى علو قدرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation says worship that night exceeds worship during a thousand months without it; its superiority comes from extra benefits, provisions, and kinds of good, not from counting the night within those months.
rows.anchor: أن العبادة فيها { خير من ألف شهر } ليس فيها هذه الليلة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid recounts an Israelite who worshipped nightly and fought by day for a thousand months; when the Prophet and Muslims admired him, the verse promised this community a better night.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : كان في بني إسرائيل رجل يقوم الليل حتى يصبح ثم يجاهد حتى يمسي

rows.speaker: مالك بن أنس
rows.claim: Malik says God gave the Prophet Laylat al-Qadr after he saw people's lifespans and feared his shorter-lived community could not match earlier nations' deeds.
rows.anchor: قال مالك بن أنس : أرى

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: In a report from Qasim ibn Fadl via Isa ibn Mazin, Hasan ibn Ali explains his pledge to Muawiya by saying the Prophet saw the Umayyads repeatedly mount his pulpit like monkeys, and the revelation identified their reign as a thousand months.
rows.anchor: رأى في منامه بني أمية يطؤن منبره واحدا بعد واحد

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi objects that praising the night by comparing it to a thousand months is unlikely if those months mean the blameworthy Umayyad reign.
rows.anchor: طعن القاضي في هذه الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentator rejects al-Qadi's objection: the Umayyad era was great in worldly happiness, so religious felicity on this night can be superior to worldly felicity then.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأن أيام بني أمية كانت أياما عظيمة بحسب السعادات الدنيوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives expansive good news because it calls the night better without measuring how much better, like the Prophet's statement about Ali's duel with Amr ibn Abd Wudd.
rows.anchor: ذكر أن هذه الليلة خير ، ولم يبين قدر الخيرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who revives the night is as though he worshipped for more than eighty-three years; doing so annually brings many lifetimes, while spending the whole month to ensure finding it is like observing thirty Qadr nights.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن من أحياها فكأنما عبد الله تعالى نيفا وثمانين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report contrasts an Israelite who worshipped four hundred years with a Muslim who worshipped forty but receives more reward: the Muslim community obeyed despite safety from immediate punishment, as in 8:33.
rows.anchor: يجاء يوم القيامة بالإسرائيلي الذي عبد الله أربعمائة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night also threatens sinners: reviving a hundred Qadr nights cannot erase punishment deserved for cheating even a grain, emphasizing the gravity of sin.
rows.anchor: إحياء مائة ليلة من القدر لا يخلصه عن ذلك العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked how one night can equal the greater effort of a thousand months despite the hadith that reward follows exertion, the commentator first says acts receive different effects according to context.
rows.anchor: صح عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : ( أجرك على قدر نصبك )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates contextual effects with congregational versus individual prayer and the same accusation of adultery: it may be true, slander warranting discretionary punishment, a charge warranting the fixed penalty, or unbelief when aimed at Aisha.
rows.anchor: فقد اختلفت الأحكام في هذه المواضع ، مع أن الصورة واحدة في الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Slandering Aisha is especially grave because it attacks her learning, the Badr veteran Safwan, all believers through the Prophet's wife, the Prophet's honor, and divine wisdom; the verse says people deemed the slander slight though God regards it as grave.
rows.anchor: قال : { وتحسبونه هينا وهو عند الله عظيم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Actions can therefore differ in reward or penalty according to their circumstances, allowing a small act to equal many acts in outward quantity.
rows.anchor: فلا يبعد أن تكون الطاعة القليلة في الصورة مساوية في الثواب للطاعات الكثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer is that God draws people to worship through multiplied rewards—twice, tenfold, seven hundredfold, and further bonuses for sacred places and times—with the aim of turning them from worldly distraction to obedience.
rows.anchor: المقصود الأصلي من الكل جر المكلف إلى الطاعة وصرفه عن الاشتغال بالدنيا

none: verse text and transition marker only

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An allegory says angels attend to spirits and humans to bodies: angels initially rejected the human spirit for lust and anger, as parents recoil from sperm and a clot; when parents see a beautiful child and angels see knowledge of God and obedience, they love the person and descend as if apologizing for their earlier objection.
rows.anchor: فهذا هو المراد من قوله : { تنزل الملائكة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When angels later see the soul amid the bodily night and darkness of physical faculties, they seek forgiveness for the believers.
rows.anchor: ويستغفرون للذين ءامنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says all angels descend to the lowest heaven; though it seems too crowded, the commentator answers that scripture's general statement takes precedence over a lone report and that they descend and ascend in waves until dawn.
rows.anchor: فلهذا السبب اختلفوا فقال بعضهم : إنها تنزل بأسرها إلى السماء الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most instead say angels descend to earth, fitting the invitation to revive the night, the reports of angels attending remembrance gatherings on other days, and the unqualified sense of descent from heaven to earth.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : وهو اختيار الأكثرين أنهم ينزلون إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among those who say they descend to earth, some say they come to witness human worship; others note that angels descend only by God's command, which by itself does not prove love.
rows.anchor: أن الملائكة قالوا : { وما نتنزل إلا بأمر ربك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘by their Lord's permission’ implies angels first sought and received permission, evidence of their longing to meet people; their standing in ranks can refer to a different time from their descent.
rows.anchor: فإنها تدل على أنهم استأذنوا أولا فأذنوا ، وذلك يدل على غاية المحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descent anticipates the afterlife, when angels greet believers through every gate; in this life, devotion brings them down to visit and greet worshippers.
rows.anchor: فههنا في الدنيا إن اشتغلت بعبادتي نزلت الملائكة عليك

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali says angels descend to greet and intercede for people, and whoever receives their greeting is forgiven.
rows.anchor: روى عن علي عليه السلام : ( أنهم ينزلون ليسلموا علينا وليشفعوا لنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels descend so that worship on earth gains greater reward, just as going to Mecca increases the reward of worship there.
rows.anchor: فهم ينزلون إلى الأرض لتصير طاعاتهم أكثر ثوابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People perform acts of worship better before eminent scholars and ascetics than alone, so the angels' presence helps make worship complete and free from deficiency.
rows.anchor: فالله تعالى أنزل الملائكة المقربين حتى أن المكلف يعلم أنه إنما يأتي بالطاعات في حضور أولئك العلماء

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb describes angels at Sidrat al-Muntaha with Gabriel: they descend on Qadr, covering every earthly place with a prostrating or standing angel praying for believers, and Gabriel greets every person.
rows.anchor: لا تبقى بقعة من الأرض إلا وعليها ملك ساجد أو قائم يدعو للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says chills, a softened heart, and tears signal Gabriel's handshake; three recitations of the testimony bring forgiveness, rescue from Hell, and entry to Paradise.
rows.anchor: من قال فيها ثلاث مرات : لا إله إلا الله غفر له بواحدة

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: After first ascending, Gabriel unfolds green wings; the angels spend the day between sun and lowest heaven praying and seeking mercy and forgiveness for believers and those who fast Ramadan faithfully.
rows.anchor: مشغولين بالدعاء والرحمة والاستغفار للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: At night the angels ask about people by name: they stop praying for one who changed from devotion to innovation, and pray for one who changed from innovation to worship; they repeat this across the heavens to the Lote tree.
rows.anchor: فيكفون عن الدعاء للأول ، ويشتغلون بالدعاء للثاني

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: The Lote tree asks about people it loves for loving God; angels list them by name and parentage, the news reaches Paradise, and Paradise, the tree, and angels pray for their arrival.
rows.anchor: فتقول لهم السدرة : يا سكاني حدثوني عن الناس فإن لي عليكم حقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A larger gathering brings more mercy; therefore the gathering of proximate angels on Laylat al-Qadr makes its mercy abundant, as at the great pilgrimage assembly.
rows.anchor: كلما كان الجمع أعظم ، كان نزول الرحمة هناك أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reported meanings of al-Ruh include a mighty angel able to swallow heaven and earth, a class of angels seen only on Qadr, a creature neither human nor angel, Jesus, the Qur'an, mercy, the noblest angel, or the recording guardians; the commentator prefers Gabriel, singled out as especially noble.
rows.anchor: والأصح أن الروح ههنا جبريل . وتخصيصه بالذكر لزيادة شرفه

rows.speaker: أبو نجيح
rows.claim: Abu Najih identifies the Spirit as the recording guardian angels: the angel on the right records obligatory good, while the one on the left records omissions of evil.
rows.anchor: عن أبي نجيح الروح هم الحفظة والكرام الكاتبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If angels know human sins, why would they long to descend? They do not see their details: they inspect the Preserved Tablet's good deeds, then a screen hides sins, prompting praise of the One who shows good and conceals evil.
rows.anchor: روى أنهم يطالعون اللوح ، فيرون فيه طاعة المكلف مفصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels also witness charitable hospitality absent in heaven: the rich bring food for the poor, who eat it while worshipping God.
rows.anchor: الأغنياء يجيئون بالطعام من بيوتهم فيجعلونه ضيافة للفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels descend to hear the moaning of sinners, which does not occur in heaven.
rows.anchor: أنهم يسمعون أنين العصاة وهذا لا يوجد في السموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A divine saying reports that the groaning of sinners is dearer to God than the praise of glorifiers, because it displays the forgiveness of the Lord of earth and heavens.
rows.anchor: لأنين المذنبين أحب إلي من زجل المسبحين
